extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media policymakers, and journalists concerned with national news policy and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evaluative criteria for national news: obstacles to innovation, journalistic functions, and standards for judging distortion and methods. Focuses on how news is produced, its social functions, and public-policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering the news in ways that 'burden' the present audience risks their departure from the readership or viewership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of limited audience research, it is impossible to predict whether innovations that make the product less accessible to the uninterested audience will cause audience loss; journalists and executives are likely correct that many existing product/audience considerations are necessary to hold the uninterested audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Some changes in the news are likely to increase pressure from sources, the vocal audience, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists have resisted pressure so far, but neither they nor executives can judge their tolerance for increased, more widespread, or more intensive pressure, nor to what extent management will protect them from escalated pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher costs
rubrics_metrics.description: News innovations requiring more staff or a larger proportion of beat reporters will raise news-organization budgets and/or require audiences to pay more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists lack sufficient power to insist on higher budgets; audiences have shown some willingness to pay more (e.g., raised subscription and newsstand prices), but television costs are hidden in advertised goods' prices; descriptive news is expensive while analytic journalism is cheaper but depends on prior descriptive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Hierarchical news organizations and cautious executives inhibit drastic innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists rise to top by being cautious; proposals for drastic change must be cleared with management, which is not paid to take unnecessary risks—this structural conservatism limits leeway.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'competitive bind'
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition among news organizations encourages offering virtually the same news, making safe conformity rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While occasional innovations break the bind (often from desperation), firms on top rarely try risky new things; rival firms avoid being too different because unsuccessful innovation leaves them defenseless against competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leeway for conservative stands, audience enlargement, and format changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have latitude to enlarge the audience, take more conservative stands, or effect format changes that repackage the basic product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are relatively low-risk changes that can please the vocal audience; however, greater substantive changes face the obstacles listed above and may be inhibited by risk-aversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on advertiser and audience income
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations' dependence on advertiser and audience revenue constrains journalistic autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To insulate themselves from pressure, journalists would have to end dependence on such income — e.g., be funded by extremely rich and independent 'angels' granting total autonomy — but such funding raises other risks (government pressure on funders) and practical problems (subpoena power, isolation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government funding/control trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Government funding or power over network profits could increase journalistic budgets yet risk governmental constraints on journalists' autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If federal government required networks to put profits into news organizations, journalists would obtain higher budgets and less need to be governed by efficiency, but government power over profits could allow it to restrain journalists from making dramatic changes that produce adverse publicity about government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative ownership models (worker control/communal ownership)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists owning and running news organizations communally or via worker control could remove commercial pressures but face questions of viability for national-scale media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worker-controlled organizations might pursue smaller, more congenial audiences and focus on analytic journalism, but serving today's large audiences competitively would likely require reinventing current news firms; a smaller interested-audience model could survive if willing to accept lower budgets and forego descriptive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for subpoena power and protection for sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: To function autonomously and obtain information without creating obligations to sources, journalists would need legal powers or protections (e.g., subpoena power) and protection from pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with independent funding, journalists would need means to compel or protect source-provided information; absent such powers, autonomy is constrained by practical access issues and social ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists as recruiters/testers of leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists play a role in winnowing political candidates and testing them for competence, public image, and honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By emphasizing campaigns and performance before cameras, television excludes candidates lacking funds or media skills; journalists test candidates' ability to answer questions, conceptualize issues, present appealing consistent images, and handle contradictions—functions that extend into administrations through continued scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as supplier of political feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: News media serve elected and appointed officials as feedback devices, indicating how the public and journalists receive actions and statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials monitor coverage (time/space, number of leads) to gauge importance attached by journalists; editorials and reporter opinions are treated as approximations of public opinion and can influence officials' decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as distributor of symbolic power
rubrics_metrics.description: By giving individuals or groups publicity (e.g., television appearances, magazine covers), news media distribute symbolic power that can become political capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicity is often ephemeral but can snowball into lasting political capital if it results in visible public or official reaction that then converts into material power over resources or decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral guardian function
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists choose moral disorder stories and frame news as morality plays, acting as watchdogs and reinforcing enduring national and societal values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This manifest function both publicizes deviance and helps punish it, thereby legitimating dominant values while repressing other values and moralities; audiences treating journalists as moral guardians enable this protective role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of religious/prophetic metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: While journalists sometimes assume roles analogous to prophets or priests, these religious metaphors overstate their moral potency and organized influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television news may function ritually or habitually, and commentators can act as long-term prophets, but journalists generally lack the concentrated, organized constituencies and enduring power of religious institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling and myth-making
rubrics_metrics.description: News transmits stories that can become myths or legends; journalists can be passive transmitters or active drafters of myth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myth status depends on journalists and future audiences; many myths are short-lived in modern societies, and whether news actually functions like pre-media storytellers depends on audience reception and journalistic agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometer of order
rubrics_metrics.description: News functions as an order barometer by selecting stories of disorder and order restoration, alerting and reassuring audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some use disorder news as early warnings; others use it to fix blame. Journalists may exaggerate the extent of disorder or the effectiveness of restorers of order. Replacement of rumor with professional news can intentionally assist officials in maintaining order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent of social control and social integration
rubrics_metrics.description: By warning against disorder, acting as moral guardians, and supplying common fare, journalists can function as agents of social control and of social integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This role can be positive (cohesion) or negative (imposing control). Empirical evidence about the news' effectiveness as a controller is limited; distrust and audience disengagement suggest possible limits to effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depoliticization/propananda risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The news media can control by depoliticizing audiences—lulling them or supplying propaganda rather than information—though claims vary across ideological perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the Left, critics argue media lull audiences into accepting status quo; on the Right, critics argue media confuse poorly educated audiences into becoming victims of propaganda. Evidence is mixed: reporting may not spur protest, but news can unintentionally facilitate movements (e.g., civil-rights movement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing nation and society
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists frame actions and statements in a national context, thereby constructing and reinforcing the reality of 'nation' and 'society'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By reporting on actors who claim to represent nation or society, journalists help impose unity and make national constructs real for audiences who live in micro-societies remote from national institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing the symbolic arena
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and news organizations manage the symbolic arena—the public stage where messages are made available—and thereby regulate who gets to place messages and who is excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management of the symbolic arena is a major political issue: in some countries government manages it; in others news organizations do so, sometimes with government veto. Who manages it bears on democratic access and public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy must be based on public values, not personal preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Public (news) policy should be justified by public values of all affected, not by the personal preferences of policymakers or scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While individual preferences shape desired news forms, public policy recommendations should proceed from prevalent public values and be argued in that normative framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: News distortion as relational standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Distortion cannot be defined absolutely; it is a relational concept judged against a specified standard (or ideal) of nondistortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards themselves are value-laden (about reality, knowledge, purposes of news, ideals of nation/society). Thus, accusations of bias/distortion must specify the standard being used (ideological balance, empirical completeness, focus on issues vs personalities, source diversity, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards are choice-laden and political
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting standards for 'undistorted' news is a political act because standards embody value judgments; actors must choose and defend standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different standards (participant observers, empirical surveys, radical perspectives) yield different judgments of distortion; universal standards are possible only via agreement on values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts are answers to questions; selection shapes news
rubrics_metrics.description: What facts become news depends on what questions are asked; facts are fashioned out of concepts and methods, which are rooted in reality and value judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists' emphasis on certain activities (e.g., campaign theatrics) preempts other significant questions (e.g., whether elections materially affect policy). Thus, distortion can arise from asking the 'wrong' questions or framing correct questions with inappropriate concepts or methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right methods and right questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation and production of news require attention to appropriate empirical methods and to selecting the 'right' questions to ask about events and actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods determine which facts are constructed; standards of empirical inquiry (scientific, participant, radical) will produce different assessments of news coverage. Choosing methods must take into account intended audiences and the democratic purposes of news.
